strengths: Originality: Extending causally selected function vectors to spatial relations in a multimodal model is a useful specialized direction. The source-conditioned weighting scheme for composing relation vectors (Equations 5–6) is an interesting hypothesis for transferring relational information.

Empirical merits: The study includes synthetic scenes and a curated GQA subset, explicitly separates training and test images, and investigates injection layer, head count, and context length. Figure 5 shows substantial gains from optimizing a single vector while freezing the backbone.

Presentation and ethics: The overall extraction, intervention, fine-tuning, and analogy pipeline is understandable and illustrated with examples. The manuscript identifies its model checkpoint and major training hyperparameters, describes dataset filtering, and discloses generative-tool use. No material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central mechanistic claims exceed the controls. Replacing head activations and improving answer probabilities establishes an intervention effect, but does not establish that those heads specifically store relational knowledge or constitute a sparse relational reasoning subnetwork. Random-head and norm-matched controls, relation-swapped interventions, image-removal or spatial-shuffling controls, and head ablations are absent. The head-count experiment also changes vector magnitude, confounding the interpretation that additional heads introduce irrelevant information.

Soundness—important numerical inconsistencies remain unexplained. Figure 5 reports synthetic zero-shot baselines around 3–6%, whereas Figures 9–10 show baselines around 26–41% for the same named relations. The appendix does not explain a different metric or evaluation setting. Figure 9's plot titles also disagree with the relation labels beneath its panels. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the connection between the ablations and main results.

Evaluation does not isolate the benefit of causal extraction. Fine-tuned vectors receive hundreds of supervised examples, whereas the principal comparison is four-shot ICL. There is no equally trained randomly initialized or zero-initialized vector, soft-prompt baseline, or comparison with the cited multimodal task-vector approach. Moreover, the zero-shot prompt provides only an image and object name, without specifying the intended relation; gains over this baseline partly reflect supplying missing task information. A relation-explicit prompt baseline is needed.

The composition evidence is insufficient for the claimed strong generalization. Section 4.4 reports only 16.8% accuracy, versus 8.3% for one-shot ICL, on synthetic diagonal relations. There are no single-component, uniform-mixture, shuffled-weight, or output-ensemble controls to distinguish compositional representations from generic steering or averaging effects. Absolute performance is approximately the 1/6 rate of uniform selection among the six pictured objects, although that is not the formal chance level of unrestricted token generation. A candidate-selection baseline would clarify practical significance.

Measurement and statistical support are weak. Accuracy checks only the first token of an object label, which can credit an incorrect full object name; collision rates and full-label accuracy are not reported. Figures provide no confidence intervals, repeated-seed variation, or statistical tests despite repeated claims of significant improvement. GQA's 200 tasks per relation reuse only 100 test images, so uncertainty should account for dependence between tasks. The validation procedure for choosing layers and head counts is also unspecified.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Appendix C claims an anonymous OSF release but supplies no identifiable repository URL in the manuscript. Equation 2 sums selected activations, whereas Section 4.1 describes averaging them, a consequential difference in intervention scale. The precise head-output projection into residual space, extraction token position, batch size, random seeds, and exact dataset splits are not sufficiently specified.

Significance and limitations: Testing one model, 32 synthetic object cutouts, and 201 highly filtered real images can support a scoped exploratory result, but does not substantiate broad conclusions about LMM modularity or transferable relational reasoning. The conclusion does not adequately acknowledge the weak absolute analogy performance or alternative explanations for the intervention gains. These evidential gaps, rather than the specialized scope itself, prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Extracting compact spatial-task representations from a multimodal model is a worthwhile interpretability problem. Updating only a relation-specific vector offers a potentially useful way to adapt a frozen model.

Empirical merits: The study includes synthetic images and a real-image GQA subset, explicitly separates training and test images, and reports substantial improvements from vector fine-tuning in Figure 5. Experiments examine injection depth, head count, and context size.

Originality: Although extraction largely follows existing function-vector methods, applying these methods to spatial relations and constructing source-conditioned mixtures for analogy transfer provides an interesting specialized extension.

Presentation and ethics: The main pipeline is understandable, with helpful prompt examples and equations. The authors acknowledge architectural and task limitations, document dataset provenance, and disclose generative-tool use. No material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—unresolved numerical inconsistency: Figure 5 reports synthetic zero-shot accuracy around 3–7% and initial-vector accuracy around 5–10%, whereas Figures 9–11 show zero-shot baselines around 28–42% and substantially higher vector accuracies for ostensibly the same synthetic tasks. The manuscript does not explain a different evaluation protocol or metric. This discrepancy makes the main results and supporting ablations difficult to reconcile.

Soundness—mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence: Mean-activation replacement establishes causal influence under the chosen intervention, but does not establish that the selected heads specifically encode spatial relations or constitute the subnetwork responsible for relational reasoning. There are no matched random-head/vector controls, cross-relation interventions, image-removal or spatial-shuffling controls, or necessity ablations. General task steering and object-label biases remain plausible explanations. Likewise, declining performance as more heads are summed could reflect intervention magnitude rather than irrelevant heads.

Soundness—comparisons do not isolate the proposed method's contribution: The zero-shot prompt supplies only an image and query object, leaving the desired relation unspecified, while the injected vector supplies relation identity. An explicit relation-instruction baseline is needed. Fine-tuned vectors additionally receive substantial supervised training that the ICL baselines do not. Training equally sized vectors from zero or random initialization would test whether causal extraction contributes beyond learning a task-specific activation offset. Figure 5 also shows that initial vectors frequently fail to improve on 4-shot ICL.

Significance and compositionality: The analogy improvement from 8.3% to 16.8% is encouraging but insufficient to establish strong generalization or linear composition of relational knowledge. Comparisons against individual constituent vectors, uniform mixtures, shuffled source weights, and output-probability ensembles are missing. These would distinguish genuine composition from selecting or averaging useful steering directions. Absolute accuracy remains low, and evaluation covers only four diagonal relations in a controlled synthetic setting.

Evaluation reliability: Accuracy measures only the first token of an object label, which does not establish correct object identification for multi-token labels. Full-label results and treatment of multiple valid GQA answers are needed. No confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, or statistical tests support repeated claims of significant improvement. The 200 tasks per GQA relation reuse only 100 test images, so uncertainty should account for dependence between tasks.

Reproducibility and presentation: Equation 2 sums selected head activations, whereas Section 4.1 describes averaging them; this changes intervention scale. The extraction token position and mapping of head outputs into the residual-stream dimension are insufficiently specified. There is no clear validation protocol for selecting injection layers and head counts. Appendix C claims an anonymous OSF release but supplies no repository address in the manuscript, preventing verification of the implementation and splits from the provided material.

Overall assessment: The spatial application has merit, and its acknowledged narrow scope is not itself disqualifying. However, the unexplained result discrepancies and missing controls undermine the central claims about localized relational representations and compositional generalization. These require substantive experimental revision before acceptance.

strengths: Originality: Applying causally selected function vectors to visual spatial relations is a useful extension of prior language and multimodal task-vector work. The source-conditioned composition of relation vectors is an interesting hypothesis for transferring relational information.

Significance: Figure 5 shows substantial improvements after fine-tuning only a compact vector while freezing the backbone, across synthetic scenes and a curated GQA subset. This suggests a potentially useful, parameter-efficient method for controlling relational predictions.

Soundness: Activation replacement provides intervention-based evidence that selected heads influence predictions. The manuscript reports image-disjoint training and evaluation sets and explores injection layer, head count, and context size.

Presentation and ethics: The main procedure is understandable, with equations and illustrative examples. The authors acknowledge the single-model and restricted-relation scope, describe dataset provenance, and disclose AI assistance. No material ethical concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—unresolved numerical inconsistency: Figure 5 reports synthetic zero-shot accuracy of approximately 0.03–0.07, whereas Figures 9–11 show zero-shot baselines around 0.26–0.42. Both are described as zero-shot relational accuracy, without explaining a different dataset, scoring rule, or conditioning regime. Figure 9 also reverses relation names between plot titles and subcaptions. These discrepancies materially undermine interpretation of the ablations and require reconciliation.

Soundness—mechanistic claims exceed the controls: Restoring correct-answer probability through activation replacement establishes causal influence, but does not establish that these heads specifically store relational knowledge or constitute the claimed causal subnetwork. Random or norm-matched head controls, mismatched-relation interventions, image-shuffling controls, and necessity tests are absent. The head-count sweep also changes the magnitude of the summed intervention, so its decline cannot uniquely establish interference from irrelevant heads.

Evaluation—insufficient baselines: Fine-tuned vectors receive substantial supervised training, while the main comparisons use only four demonstrations. Training an identically sized vector from zero or random initialization is essential to establish the value of causal extraction. Comparisons with existing multimodal task-vector methods and a matched lightweight adaptation baseline are missing. Furthermore, the bare zero-shot prompt omits the desired relation, while the selected vector supplies it; an explicit relation-instruction baseline would make that comparison informative.

Generalization—the composition claim is not isolated: Figure 6 improves accuracy from 8.3% to 16.8%, but lacks comparisons with uniform vector averaging, the highest-weight individual vector, and prediction-level mixtures. Consequently, the gain does not establish that linear composition represents a novel diagonal relation rather than selecting or averaging useful cardinal-relation behavior. Absolute performance remains low, and first-token correctness alone does not demonstrate reliable object identification.

Statistical evidence is inadequate: Claims of significant improvements are unsupported by confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical tests. GQA evaluation samples 200 tasks per relation from only 100 images and 792 relation instances overall, creating dependence and repeated examples that should be accounted for. Figure 5 also appears to show approximately equal performance for fine-tuning and four-shot ICL on GQA 'below,' despite the blanket claim of outperforming all baselines.

Reproducibility: Appendix C promises an anonymous OSF repository but supplies no identifiable URL. The manuscript does not clearly specify the extraction token position, projection of head outputs into the residual space, or validation protocol for choosing intervention layers and head counts. Equation 2 sums head activations, whereas Section 4.1 describes averaging them; this affects intervention scale. These omissions impede faithful reproduction.

Overall significance: The specialized setting is reasonable, but the central claims of localized relational knowledge and strong compositional generalization remain insufficiently supported. The promising empirical gains do not outweigh the unresolved evaluation inconsistencies and missing controls needed for acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Compact interventions for visual relational reasoning are potentially useful. Figure 6 shows substantial improvements from fine-tuning a single vector while freezing the backbone, particularly for Qwen3-VL.

Empirical scope: The study covers two architectures, synthetic spatial tasks, and spatial and agentic relations in real GQA images. Held-out-object evaluation is valuable: Qwen3-VL reaches 72.2% with fine-tuned vectors versus 21.3% with ICL.

Originality: Extending function vectors to visual relations and inferring composition weights from an analogy example constitute a useful application and an interesting generalization hypothesis. Composite vectors improve Qwen3-VL accuracy from 28.7% with four-shot ICL to 45.1%.

Presentation and responsibility: The main workflow is understandable, with helpful prompt and composition diagrams. The manuscript acknowledges its restricted relation coverage and dependence on demonstrations, and discusses potential misuse. No material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Activation replacement establishes an intervention effect, but does not establish that selected heads specifically encode relational knowledge or constitute the sparse subnetwork responsible for reasoning. There are no matched random-head controls, wrong-relation interventions, head-ablation necessity tests, or image-removal controls. Fine-tuning an unrestricted residual vector further separates the performance gains from the proposed head-level mechanism.

Soundness—baseline comparisons do not isolate the contribution. Section 3.3.3 explicitly gives the zero-shot baseline only an image and object name, leaving the intended relation unspecified, whereas selecting a relation-specific vector supplies that information. Explicit relation-instruction baselines are needed. Comparisons against equally trained vectors initialized randomly or at zero, and against parameter-efficient alternatives, are also necessary to determine whether causal extraction contributes beyond supervised adaptation.

Soundness—composition remains underdetermined. The diagonal-relation experiments lack strongest-single-vector selection, uniform-mixture, and prediction-level ensemble controls. Consequently, improved accuracy does not distinguish genuinely composed relational representations from selecting or averaging useful base-task interventions. The manuscript also does not clearly identify whether the component vectors in these experiments are initial or fine-tuned.

Evaluation validity: Accuracy measures only the first token of the object label (Section 3.3.3), which can count incorrect object names sharing a prefix as correct. Full-label evaluation and handling of multiple valid GQA answers are needed. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results support the repeated claims of significant improvement; GQA's resampled tasks also reuse a relatively small image pool.

Presentation and consistency: Figures 11–13 show synthetic zero-shot baselines around 27–41%, which are not reconciled with Table 1 or Figure 14, and their model identity is unclear. Section 4.3 reports 1,413 agentic test images, whereas Appendix A.2 specifies 706. Appendix D claims fine-tuned vectors outperform all baselines across relations, yet Figure 15 shows OpenFlamingo carrying performance below four-shot ICL. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the reported evaluation.

Reproducibility: Equation 2 sums head activations, whereas Section 4.1 describes averaging them; the projection into a common residual-space representation is unspecified. The corruption procedure describes only four cardinal relations despite experiments with seven spatial and five agentic relations. Validation-based layer/head selection, batch size, seeds, and complete model-specific intervention settings are not supplied. The claimed GitHub release has no usable address in the manuscript.

Overall significance and originality are constrained by these unresolved issues. The extraction procedure closely follows prior function-vector work, so convincing new mechanistic understanding or controlled evidence of compositional generalization is central to acceptance. The promising adaptation results do not yet substantiate those stronger contributions.

strengths: Significance: Compact interventions for visual relational reasoning are useful, and the reported fine-tuning gains warrant further investigation. Qwen3-VL achieves 72.2% on held-out synthetic objects versus 21.3% for ICL, and composite vectors achieve 45.1% versus 28.7% for four-shot ICL.

Experimental scope: The study includes two architectures, synthetic spatial tasks, natural-image spatial and agentic relations, held-out objects, and synthetic-to-GQA transfer. Image-disjoint evaluation and object holdouts provide meaningful evidence beyond training-example memorization.

Originality: Applying function vectors to visual relations and constructing source-conditioned mixtures for analogy is a potentially useful extension of existing function-vector and multimodal task-vector work, although the underlying extraction method is largely inherited.

Presentation and ethics: The main pipeline is understandable, with helpful diagrams and explicit objectives. The limitations appropriately acknowledge restricted relation coverage and the need for a source analogy. The impact statement discusses misuse, including surveillance; I identify no material ethical concern in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—baseline comparability: The zero-shot prompt contains only an image and query-object label (Section 3.3.3), so it does not identify which relation to apply. The injected vector supplies that missing information. Beating this baseline therefore does not establish improved relational reasoning. An explicit relation-instruction baseline is essential. Furthermore, fine-tuned vectors receive substantial supervised training whereas the main comparators receive four demonstrations. Matched-data learned-vector or soft-prompt baselines, including random or zero initialization, are needed to establish the value of causal extraction.

Soundness—mechanistic interpretation: Activation replacement demonstrates causal influence under the chosen intervention, but does not establish that the selected heads specifically encode visual relations or constitute the localized mechanism responsible for relational reasoning. There are no matched random-head, wrong-relation-vector, image-shuffling, or selected-head ablation controls separating relational computation from answer priors and generic task steering. Figure 6 also shows initial vectors below four-shot ICL across the reported model/dataset combinations. The strongest improvements follow supervised optimization of an unrestricted residual vector, which does not validate the original head-localization claim.

Soundness—compositionality: Figure 7 compares weighted mixtures against ICL, but not against selecting the single best source-scoring vector, uniform mixtures, or combining output probabilities rather than hidden vectors. These controls are necessary to distinguish genuinely useful vector composition from routing among existing skills or ensembling. Whether the base vectors are extracted or fine-tuned is also insufficiently explicit. Four diagonal synthetic relations support a limited proof of concept, rather than the broad claim of strong generalization to untrained relations.

Evaluation validity: Accuracy measures only whether the highest-ranked next token matches the first token of the target object label (Section 3.3.3), rather than whether the complete object is identified. This can conflate different multi-token labels, particularly on GQA. The manuscript should report complete-label accuracy, address multiple valid relational answers, and include uncertainty across extraction/training seeds. Repeated sampling of 1,000 tasks per relation from small image pools also requires accounting for shared images when estimating uncertainty.

Reproducibility: Important implementation choices remain unresolved. Equation 2 sums head activations, whereas Section 4.1 describes averaging them; the distinction changes intervention magnitude. Projection of individual head outputs into the residual space is not specified. The balanced corruption procedure describes only four cardinal relations, leaving its application to seven spatial and five agentic GQA relations unclear. Validation-based selection of layers and head counts, batch size, and seeds are not documented. The claimed GitHub release has no visible URL in the supplied manuscript.

Presentation and evidential consistency: Section 4.3 calls all 1,413 agentic images test images, whereas Appendix A.2 specifies 707 training and 706 test images. Figure 11's zero-shot baselines are approximately 27–41% across cardinal relations, which is not reconciled with Table 1's synthetic averages of 4.8% and 19.5%; the model and evaluation setting need clarification. Claims that fine-tuned vectors consistently outperform every baseline also conflict with the OpenFlamingo carrying result in Figure 15. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the otherwise promising results.

strengths: Significance: Training a single relation-specific vector while freezing the backbone is a potentially useful way to control multimodal models. The reported gains are substantial for Qwen3-VL, including 72.2% accuracy on held-out synthetic objects versus 21.3% for ICL and 23.3% for the initial vector (Section 4.3).

Soundness: Evaluation covers two different model architectures, controlled synthetic scenes, and natural images with spatial and agentic relations. Held-out objects and synthetic-to-GQA transfer provide useful evidence beyond performance on the extraction distribution.

Originality: Extending function vectors to visual relations and inferring vector-mixture weights from a source analogy is an interesting application of existing ideas. The composite-vector results, including 45.1% versus 28.7% for four-shot Qwen3-VL, warrant further investigation.

Presentation and ethics: The main pipeline is understandable, with helpful prompt and analogy illustrations. The paper acknowledges its restricted relation coverage and dependence on source demonstrations, and discusses potential misuse in surveillance. No material ethical concern is apparent from the described research.
weaknesses: Soundness—central mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Increasing correct-answer probability through activation replacement demonstrates an intervention effect, but does not establish that relational knowledge is localized in the selected heads or that those heads are necessary for relational reasoning. There are no matched random-head/vector controls, wrong-relation interventions, or necessity ablations. Figure 6 also shows that initial extracted vectors generally underperform four-shot ICL; the strongest results follow supervised optimization, which can introduce task information rather than merely expose an existing mechanism.

Evaluation—baselines do not isolate the proposed contribution. Section 3.3.3 explicitly defines the zero-shot prompt as an image and query object without specifying the desired relation, making the task underdetermined for the unmodified model. Relation-specific vectors supply that missing information. The paper needs an explicit relation-instruction baseline and a matched-data baseline that trains a randomly or zero-initialized vector at the same layer. Without these, comparisons against zero-shot and four-shot ICL cannot establish the benefit of causal extraction over ordinary supervised task conditioning.

Evaluation—the reported metric is first-token agreement, not correct object identification (Section 3.3.3). Distinct multi-token object labels can share an initial token, particularly in GQA. Full-label accuracy, treatment of multiple valid answers, and image-ablated or shuffled-image controls are needed to establish that the gains reflect grounded relational prediction rather than label priors or partial-name matches.

Originality and generalization—the analogy experiment does not distinguish compositional reasoning from selection or averaging of existing predictors. Relevant controls include selecting the highest-weight base vector, uniform vector averaging, and combining predictions instead of hidden vectors. The manuscript also does not clearly specify whether the composite vectors use initial or fine-tuned constituents. Consequently, the reported improvement supports the usefulness of the procedure more strongly than the claim that linear combinations represent new relations.

Reproducibility—important implementation and selection details remain ambiguous. Equation 2 sums head activations whereas Section 4.1 describes averaging them, and the mapping from head outputs to residual-stream dimensions is unspecified. The four-relation corruption procedure does not explain its application to GQA's seven spatial and five agentic relations. No separate validation protocol is given for choosing layers and head counts. Section 4.3 lists 1,413 agentic test images, whereas Appendix A.2 specifies 706; this requires clarification, although it does not itself establish leakage.

Evidence and presentation—results lack repeated-run uncertainty or confidence intervals despite repeated claims of significant improvements. Some appendix results are difficult to reconcile with the main evaluation: Figure 11 shows synthetic zero-shot baselines around 0.3–0.4 without identifying a model or setting that explains their difference from Table 1. These ambiguities, together with the missing controls, prevent reliable assessment of the central claims. The promising empirical gains do not yet provide sufficient support for acceptance.
